findings.title: Google refresh persists the Zod wrapper and breaks the credential
findings.body: GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken now saves the return value of parseRefreshTokenResponse as credential.key. That helper returns Zod's safeParse result, {success: true, data: ...}, not the token object. The previous code stored googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials). This runs on every expiry refresh whether or not credential sharing is enabled. After the first successful refresh (access tokens last about an hour), the row no longer matches googleCredentialSchema, which is parsed again in the constructor at the next GoogleCalendarService load. Availability, event create/update/delete, and Meet links then throw for that linked credential. Reconnecting creates a new credential row and does not repair the existing id already attached to destination calendars, so the broken row keeps being selected. When sharing is enabled the same function fails earlier: refreshOAuthTokens returns a Fetch Response with no .data, token.access_token throws, and the catch treats every error other than invalid_grant as success and returns the expired client without writing a new token.

findings.title: Refresh parser invents refresh_token and strips real token fields
findings.body: After a successful parse, parseRefreshTokenResponse sets data.refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token" whenever the field is missing, and callers persist that object. Office365CalendarService spreads the parsed data over the stored credential. Its schema marks refresh_token optional, and Microsoft's token endpoint is allowed to omit a new refresh token while the previous one stays valid. The spread then replaces the real refresh token with "refresh_token", so the next refresh fails until the user reconnects. This is not limited to the new sync flag. When sharing is enabled the schema used instead is also wrong: the computed keys z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() are one literal property (both are typically "[object Object]", so the second overwrites the first), not a wildcard, and Zod strips unknown keys. expires_in, expiry_date, refresh_token, scope, and instance_url are dropped, then the placeholder refresh token is added. Office 365 and Zoom write that result back; Zoom also sets expiry_date from a missing expires_in, which is NaN, and zoomTokenSchema rejects NaN on the next read. Salesforce would persist the stripped object once its missing prisma import is fixed. The comment that any numeric property is the expiry is not implemented.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh calls prisma without importing it
findings.body: The new getClient path calls prisma.credential.update, but this file never imports prisma. Every other adapter in the PR imports @calcom/prisma explicitly, so this is not a global. SalesforceCalendarService constructs this.conn by calling getClient, so the first Salesforce calendar operation throws ReferenceError before a jsforce connection is returned. Event create, update, delete, and contact sync fail for every Salesforce user as soon as this code runs, including deployments that never enable credential sync.

findings.title: Salesforce always refreshes against production and then uses the old access token
findings.body: getClient now always POSTs to https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token and throws unless statusText is exactly "OK", before it builds the connection. Sandbox orgs must refresh at test.salesforce.com, and My Domain orgs use their own token URL; those refreshes fail and abort the client even when the stored access token is still valid. Previously a valid access token was used directly. The jsforce Connection is then created with credentialKey.access_token, the pre-refresh value, not the access token just returned, so an already-expired token is what this request uses. The refresh also ignores refreshOAuthTokens, so CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is never consulted for Salesforce. The value written back is accessTokenParsed.data; with sharing enabled that object has been reduced to access_token plus a fabricated refresh_token, so instance_url and the other Salesforce fields are dropped from the saved key.

findings.title: Sync refresh returns an unchecked Fetch Response that callers treat as a provider token
findings.body: When sharing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw Fetch Response and does not check response.ok, parse JSON, or set a timeout. Callers were not updated to that contract, and the comment says the body should only be an access token and expiry, which is not what they read. HubSpot, Zoho CRM, and Zoho Bigin expect an axios or HubSpot SDK object and read .data, .accessToken, or .expiresIn. HubSpot then passes that Response to prisma.credential.update as key; JSON serialization keeps only the own property expiryDate (NaN becomes null), so the stored HubSpot credential is wiped to {expiryDate: null}. Google reads res.data, throws, and its catch swallows every error except invalid_grant, leaving the expired token in place. MS Teams parses the body and replaces the entire credential key with it, dropping refresh_token and email. Lark, Webex, and Zoom feed the same response into handlers that require the provider envelope; a non-OK or invalid_grant-shaped sync error can mark the Zoom or Webex credential invalid. A hung sync URL blocks booking and availability indefinitely because fetch has no timeout.

findings.title: Token sync request sends user id with no authentication
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, an HMAC, or any other credential, and it does not require the URL to be https. That endpoint is expected to return OAuth access tokens. The parent app therefore cannot tell Cal.com from any other caller who can reach the URL, and a client that can reach it can request tokens for arbitrary user ids. An http:// endpoint value would also put bearer tokens on the wire in cleartext. Nothing in .env.example says the caller is unauthenticated. The response is trusted with no status check, so an error body can be stored as a credential.

findings.title: Lark deletes the credential before the sync refresh can run
findings.body: refreshAccessToken still deletes the credential and throws when the stored refresh token is missing or refresh_expires_date is expired. That check runs before the new refreshOAuthTokens call. With credential sync the parent is the source of truth, and the sync helper documents a response that only contains an access token and expiry, so the local refresh token may be absent or already expired. In that case Cal.com deletes the Lark row instead of asking CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT for a new access token. The connection is gone and later calendar calls fail until the user reconnects; a webhook replay cannot help if the row was removed and a later findFirst misses the replacement.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sync sends the credential id as the Cal.com user id
findings.body: BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken passes credentialId, the Credential primary key, as the third argument of refreshOAuthTokens. That argument is posted as calcomUserId. Credential ids and user ids are independent sequences, so when sync is enabled the parent looks up tokens for the wrong person and can return another user's Zoho access token. The Bigin code then reads tokenInfo.data as if the result were an axios response. A Fetch Response has no .data, so refresh throws and Bigin calls fail. If the response parsing is fixed without fixing the id, the other user's token would be written onto this credential.

findings.title: Zoom sync asks for app slug zoomvideo but credentials are stored as zoom
findings.body: Zoom's refresh calls refreshOAuthTokens with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the OAuth callback in this PR stores the credential with appId "zoom" and the install path uses slug "zoom". When credential sync is enabled, the parent is queried for zoomvideo and will not find the Zoom tokens it stored or received under zoom. Refresh fails and Zoom meetings cannot be created for synced users even when the webhook wrote a valid credential.

findings.title: Credential sync upsert is racy and can leave a stale duplicate
findings.body: The webhook does findFirst({userId, appId}) and then either updates that id or creates a row. Those steps are not in a transaction, and Credential has no unique constraint on (userId, appId). The Lark callback in this PR already notes that userId and type are not unique, which is why that flow updates by credential id. Two concurrent deliveries, including a parent retry, can both see no row and both insert, or findFirst can update an arbitrary duplicate because there is no orderBy. Calendar code also uses findFirst, so it can keep using a stale credential while the webhook returns 200. A retried sync therefore does not reliably make the parent the source of truth.

findings.title: Synced credentials are not unmarked invalid
findings.body: When a credential already exists, the webhook updates only key. It does not set invalid to false. Google, Webex, and Zoom in this PR set invalid true so a failed refresh stops being used. A parent that pushes a replacement token for a credential Cal.com already marked invalid still gets 200, but loaders that skip invalid rows will ignore the new keys and the integration stays disconnected.

findings.title: Webhook throws on bad input and stores decrypted keys with no shape check
findings.body: The handler has no method check and no try/catch around zod parse, symmetricDecrypt, or JSON.parse. A non-POST, a missing body, a string userId (the schema is z.number(), not coerce), or a ciphertext that does not decrypt to JSON becomes an unhandled 500, and the crypto or parser message can be returned to the caller. The decrypted value is written straight into credential.key. An array, string, or unexpected object is accepted, so a buggy parent can persist a shape the app later casts and crashes on, with a 200 only if Prisma happens to accept it.

findings.title: Privileged credential webhook uses a raw reusable secret
findings.body: This route can replace any user's integration credential, including calendar, video, CRM, and Stripe payment keys, for any app slug. The only check is inequality against a static header value. The compare is not constant-time, the secret is the raw header rather than an HMAC over the body, and there is no timestamp or nonce. A captured request stays valid forever and also discloses the secret itself, so the holder can forge new writes for every userId, not only replay one body. Rolling a rotated token back is enough to keep using a stolen OAuth refresh token after the parent thought it had replaced it.

findings.title: No tests for credential sync or the OAuth refresh persistence change
findings.body: The diff adds a privileged webhook and changes token refresh for every major OAuth app, but there are no new tests, and the PR checklist says tests were not added. The manual plan only hits the webhook and a simulated sync refresh. A unit test that refreshes Google and Office 365 with sharing disabled and asserts the stored key is still the token object, with the previous refresh_token kept when the provider omits one, would have caught the universal credential corruption. The webhook also has no coverage for a wrong secret, a non-object decrypted payload, an invalid credential being cleared, or two concurrent creates.
